subject: chemistry

moments.title: The Karlsruhe Congress
moments.body:
Chemistry in 1860 has no agreed atomic masses. The same element gets different values in different labs. Stanislao Cannizzaro distributes a pamphlet at the Karlsruhe Congress that revives Avogadro's hypothesis and gives consistent atomic masses.

Among the delegates: a 26-year-old Russian named Dmitri Mendeleev. He reads Cannizzaro's pamphlet and starts trying to organise the elements.
moments.takeaway: Without agreed atomic masses, no periodic table was possible. Karlsruhe gave chemistry a foundation.

moments.title: Mendeleev's first periodic table
moments.body:
Mendeleev is writing a chemistry textbook. He sketches out the 63 known elements in order of atomic mass and notices that similar properties recur regularly. He published his table in the journal of the Russian Chemical Society in March 1869.

Mendeleev's audacity: where his pattern required an element that didn't exist, he LEFT A GAP and predicted its properties.

quote.text: We must expect the discovery of many yet unknown elements — for example, two analogues of boron and aluminium with atomic weights 65 and 75.

moments.takeaway: Mendeleev didn't just classify what was known — he predicted what wasn't.

moments.title: Gallium, scandium, germanium
moments.body:
Lecoq de Boisbaudran discovers gallium spectroscopically (1875). Its properties match Mendeleev's predicted 'eka-aluminium' almost exactly — including atomic mass 69.7 (predicted 68), density 5.9 (predicted 5.9), and forming a 3+ chloride.

Scandium (1879) matches 'eka-boron'. Germanium (1886) matches 'eka-silicon'. Three predictions, three confirmations within Mendeleev's lifetime.
moments.takeaway: Predicting unknown elements transformed Mendeleev's table from a classification into a scientific theory.

moments.title: Moseley reorders by atomic number
moments.body:
Mendeleev had ordered elements by atomic mass, but the order felt 'wrong' in places (tellurium before iodine, despite tellurium being heavier). Henry Moseley measured the X-ray spectra of elements and showed each element has a characteristic 'atomic number' (proton count) that gives the true sequence.

Moseley was killed at Gallipoli in 1915, aged 27. His death prompted the British government to restrict young scientists from front-line combat.

quote.text: Now the elements can be examined one by one in their proper order, even when the atomic weights make hash of the order.

moments.takeaway: Atomic number, not mass, is the periodic table's true organising principle.

now.title: The table today
now.body:
118 elements are now confirmed — the last (oganesson) named in 2016. Synthesis of superheavy elements happens at heavy-ion colliders in Dubna (Russia), GSI (Germany), and Berkeley (USA), one or a few atoms at a time.

The periodic table's structure is explained by quantum mechanics: shells, subshells and electron configurations. Mendeleev's empirical patterns are direct consequences of orbital filling rules.
now.open_questions: How far can the table extend? Predictions of an 'island of stability' near element 114 or 126 suggest some superheavy elements might be (relatively) stable. Element 119 has been searched for since 2007 but never confirmed. Is there a fundamental upper limit to atomic number?

reflection: Mendeleev was passed over for the Nobel Prize in 1906 (by one vote, in favour of Henri Moissan for isolating fluorine). He died in 1907. How should scientific recognition deal with achievements that pre-date the prize?
